From: Antoine Guisan [antoine...@unil.ch]

To: Antoine Guisan
Subject: FW: First Assistant (Postdoc) in Spatial Modelling of Species and Biodiversity

Dear colleagues,

I am looking for an experienced modeler for a postdoc position available for up to 3 years in my lab in Lausanne. Thanks to circulate this information to any potential candidate.

Best wishes

Antoine

First Assistant (Postdoc) in Spatial Modelling of Species and Biodiversity

Introduction

UNIL is a leading international teaching and research institution, with over 5,000 employees and 15,500 students split between its Dorigny campus, CHUV and Epalinges. As an employer, UNIL encourages excellence, individual recognition and responsibility.

Presentation

The Institute of Earth Surface Dynamics (IDYST) of the Faculty of Geosciences & Environment is opening a position as First Assistant (Postdoc) in Spatial Modelling of Species and Biodiversity.

Job information

Expected start date in position : 01.09.2020

Contract length : 1 year, renewable 1 x 2 years, maximum 3 years

Activity rate : 100%

Workplace : Lausanne Dorigny (Géopolis)

Your responsibilities

100% of the activity will be dedicated to research in the ValPar.CH project, within the Spatial Ecology group (ECOSPAT <http://www.unil.ch/ecospat>) in the GSE Faculty, IDYST institute.

Your qualifications

The candidate will have already a PhD grade and work within the new multidisciplinary national project ValPar.CH aiming at evaluating and modelling habitats, biodiversity and ecosystem services in Switzerland and for selected parks of national importance.

The candidate will be particularly involved in the spatial modelling of species and biodiversity at both the national scale and within parks at fine resolution. This task will require intensive and efficient computing, thus the candidate is expected to have advanced experience in computer programming, statistics and simulations, and a good knowledge in biogeography, especially about the drivers of species distributions.

The project will be based on existing national species occurrence data and environmental maps, so that no sampling will be required.

The candidate will also have to collaborate with the other researchers within the project, and especially with those involved in habitat and landuse mapping.

English will be the language for the scientific part of the project, but knowledge of French and German would be a plus.

What the position offers you

We offer a nice working place in a multicultural, diverse and dynamic academic environment. Opportunities for professional training, a lot of activities and other benefits to discover.

Contact for further information

Mr

Professor

Antoine Guisan

Antoine...@unil.ch

Your application

Deadline : 30.06.2020

Please, send your application with a motivation letter, CV, copy of the PhD diploma (not the thesis itself), publication list with a short statement of research achievements, the coordinates and emails of 3 reference persons in Word or PDF.
Only applications through this website will be taken into account.

We thank you for your understanding.

Additional information

UNIL is committed to equal opportunities and diversity.
www.unil.ch/egalite <https://www.unil.ch/egalite/en/home.html>

UNIL supports early career researchers.
www.unil.ch/graduatecampus <https://unil.ch/graduatecampus/en/home.html>

Dear all,

I would appreciate help to spread the ad for this postdoc position. (Sorry for post-crossing.)

Modelling and predicting metacommunity dynamics

Duties: You will develop models for spatial metacommunity dynamics of epiphytes or deadwood fungi. We have extensive data on the colonization-extinction dynamics of most metacommunity members in both study systems. The modelling will test for effects of environmental conditions, species interactions, species traits and phylogenies. There is also possibility to do fieldwork. Finally, you will make projections of metacommunity dynamics assuming scenarios. We study how socio-economic policy, climate change or forest management on different spatial scales (global, EU, landscape) may affect the future delivery of ecosystem services and metacommunity structure of different organism groups. The work is funded by The Swedish Research Council and by Formas.

messages.subject: What exactly is availability and when should we use the superpopulation or available population estimate for density?
messages.subject_clean: What exactly is availability and when should we use the superpopulation or available population estimate for density?
messages.body_plain:
This is a set of general questions for the group that may apply to many circumstances but in my case, I am working with distance sampling of ungulates on line transects.  In my case, I have repeated surveys along transects that allow for estimation of availability within periods where I assume the population is closed.  This allows me to derive an estimate of the superpopulation and the available population within the transect strip.  I can estimate density with either of these population estimates, but following the discussion in Kery and Royle 2016 (p485) the one I should use depends on whether availability is driven by spatial vs random temporary emigration (individuals temporarily out of the transect strip vs individuals hiding within the strip).  They acknowledge that both processes may be occurring simultaneously and it should be possible to model both.  However, in the absence of such a model...
1. Are there general rules for resolving whether movement or hiding might be more strongly driving availability for a particular species and survey method?
2. Does hiding including individuals with very low detection probabilities?  One example often used is animals in burrows, but what about completely stationary animals with great camouflage? Animals in dense bushes?  There seems to be some potential for overlap between availability process and the detection process in the case of random temp emigration.
2. In the case of distance sampling, would selecting for a larger strip widths (truncating fewer observations) tend to increase, decrease, or have no effect on the degree to which each availability process affects estimates.   I am inclined to think that a larger proportion of the population be completely contained by larger strip widths and the role of spatial temporary emigration should be decrease with wider strips.

For some context, in the study systems where we work, observations out to 1 km are possible for species that can also have very large and very small home ranges.

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Thank you for raising such an interesting topic for discussion.

I've been working with availability and perception bias in a distance sampling context for cetaceans (whale and dolphins) and I have identified overlap between both biases in the literature and also in the way we're modelling them.
Here is what I found of most relevance to distinguish between both

1) First of all, define the object unit you're working with. For cetaceans the unit is group (or cluster) rather than individual. So when we model detection and availability we should make sure we are modelling the "probability of detecting a group" and "probability of a group being available".

2) Define availability in your species-specific context. For example, we define an object (group) as available whether at least one individual of the group is available to be detected. In our context we've considered a group of whales that are subsurface but still have a chance of being detected (even though the chance is very small). In this process it's interesting to account for covariates that have potential effects on availability. For example, group size, group composition, water transparency. Maybe in your case it could be "bush density" or "level of camouflage".

3) I am not sure how to distinguish between "spatial" and "temporary" emigration. My guess is that in practice those definitions are related to the sampling window you have while doing distance sampling. If you estimate availability on the trackline (y=0), the calculation of the sampling window basically depends on the radius forward the observer and survey platform speed.

Look forward to hearing more about that!

Kind regards,
Heloise

messages.body_plain:
Heloise,
I think you hit on some key points, the most important being that the behavior matters.  I should note that I cannot distinquish individuals, so I don't have the power of recaptures to estimate availability or detection.  Similar to you, I am dealing with groups, but I think groups may be less cohesive in ungulates than in cetaceans, but detection of individuals is dependent on detection of others.  In my case I am modelling detection and availability of  groups.  Just to clarify, are you using 'perceptibility' to refer to the product of availability and detectibility?

You hit on an interesting idea.   Kery and Royle state that hiding might be a form of random temp emigration.  This particularly type of availability should be 1 on the transect line (for ungulates that can't burrow...except warthogs!).  Might it be possible to model this form of random temp emigration similarly to detectability, as a process that increases with distance from the transect line (inverse hazard, half-normal form, etc) ?  Additionally, repeat samples might show variation in counts immediately along the transect line (at distance = 0) that contain information regarding spatial temp emigration because variation in such repeat counts should be partially driven by individuals that are temporarily away (and can't possibly be hiding).

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Sorry, I use the terms perception and detection interchangeably.

Do you mean you have multiple single-platform (single-observer) distance sampling surveys?
What is the time between consecutive surveys? I think this will answer what kind of availability you could estimate from your data. If the time between surveys is greater than the 'hiding time', you have means to estimate spatial emigration only.

I don't think you can estimate availability as random temporary emigration from distance sampling only data. In some cases you could do that from mark-recapture distance sampling, but most of the time you need a different survey to do focal follows of groups. Again, it depends on the species behaviour and type of survey platform/sampling window.

Hope this helps somehow :)

Kind regards,
Heloise

messages.subject: Re: What exactly is availability and when should we use the superpopulation or available population estimate for density?
messages.subject_clean: What exactly is availability and when should we use the superpopulation or available population estimate for density?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

That's an interesting discussion! I have been working with aerial transects to survey ungulates and in my case, I clearly have the possibility of unavailability of individuals (in distance zero) by being hidden below vegetation. In this case, random temporary emigration is the process related to hidden individuals (maybe equivalent to submerged cetaceans in the context mentioned by Heloise) and spatial temporary emigration is the process related to individuals entering and leaving the sites between occasions.

I think if you can assume that the overall detection probability (perception AND availability) is one at distance zero, I would not matter with temporary emigration (spatial or random) and would derive density estimates from the population estimates for each occasion (and not from the superpopulation). Then, I think that individuals that you may lose by being hidden behind vegetation in other distances (other than zero) would be accommodated in the detection process, related to distance.

If you cannot assume perfect detection at zero distance (I don't think this is the case for terrestrial transects of ungulates), I think you would need extra information to properly address availability error, such as a double observer protocol, as said by Heloise.

Best wishes,

Ismael

I think you might be right that if the time in between surveys (here, it is weeks) is longer than the 'hiding time' than phi may be most likley estimating temporal spatial emigration, but is is not quite clear why short hiding times relative to inter-replicate intervals would imply an inability to estimate hiding-based availability.  Intuitively it seems to make sense that a double observer protocol would reveal individuals who are coming in and out of hiding on short time scales. messages.subject: Re: What exactly is availability and when should we use the superpopulation or available population estimate for density?
messages.subject_clean: What exactly is availability and when should we use the superpopulation or available population estimate for density?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ismael, Your example makes sense to me, where the individuals on the transect line are more or less beyond the scope of the detector (you in the plane).  It is physically impossible to see them.  Beyond that distance and in other survey protocols where perception is 1 at distance 0, I think what we may be talking about is spatial variation in random temporary emigration within a site.  Further, are we saying that this spatial variation in rand temp emigration (hiding) is not driven by the behavior or ecology of the animal, but is driven t by the attributes of the detector?  I think if this is the case, we are talking about perception, not availability.  Perhaps the critical issue is that if the probability of detecting a 'hider' is  always non-zero, even if it is incredibly small, than we are talking about perception, not random temp emigration.   The confusion I think I am having is with distance sampling where at the outer bounds of the truncated observation distances, there are very likley groups that are completely obscured and this must be true in all distance sampling surveys.  If this isn't true, than there really are no 'pure' hiders in the survey (no individuals or groups with 0 probability of being perceived) and if availability is found to be <1, than it must all be spatial temp emigration and only the available population should be used in estimating density (not the superpopulation).

I am benefiting very much from hearing everyone's thoughts on this.

> That's an interesting discussion! I have been working with aerial transects to survey ungulates and in my case, I clearly have the possibility of unavailability of individuals (in distance zero) by being hidden below vegetation. In this case, random temporary emigration is the process related to hidden individuals (maybe equivalent to submerged cetaceans in the context mentioned by Heloise) and spatial temporary emigration is the process related to individuals entering and leaving the sites between occasions.
>
> I think if you can assume that the overall detection probability (perception AND availability) is one at distance zero, I would not matter with temporary emigration (spatial or random) and would derive density estimates from the population estimates for each occasion (and not from the superpopulation). Then, I think that individuals that you may lose by being hidden behind vegetation in other distances (other than zero) would be accommodated in the detection process, related to distance.
>
> If you cannot assume perfect detection at zero distance (I don't think this is the case for terrestrial transects of ungulates), I think you would need extra information to properly address availability error, such as a double observer protocol, as said by Heloise.
>
> Best wishes,
>
> Ismael
>
> Em quarta-feira, 10 de junho de 2020 22:21:42 UTC-3, David Christianson escreveu:
> > This is a set of general questions for the group that may apply to many circumstances but in my case, I am working with distance sampling of ungulates on line transects.  In my case, I have repeated surveys along transects that allow for estimation of availability within periods where I assume the population is closed.  This allows me to derive an estimate of the superpopulation and the available population within the transect strip.  I can estimate density with either of these population estimates, but following the discussion in Kery and Royle 2016 (p485) the one I should use depends on whether availability is driven by spatial vs random temporary emigration (individuals temporarily out of the transect strip vs individuals hiding within the strip).  They acknowledge that both processes may be occurring simultaneously and it should be possible to model both.  However, in the absence of such a model...
> > 1. Are there general rules for resolving whether movement or hiding might be more strongly driving availability for a particular species and survey method?
> > 2. Does hiding including individuals with very low detection probabilities?  One example often used is animals in burrows, but what about completely stationary animals with great camouflage? Animals in dense bushes?  There seems to be some potential for overlap between availability process and the detection process in the case of random temp emigration.
> > 2. In the case of distance sampling, would selecting for a larger strip widths (truncating fewer observations) tend to increase, decrease, or have no effect on the degree to which each availability process affects estimates.   I am inclined to think that a larger proportion of the population be completely contained by larger strip widths and the role of spatial temporary emigration should be decrease with wider strips.
> >
> > For some context, in the study systems where we work, observations out to 1 km are possible for species that can also have very large and very small home ranges.
messages.body_snippet: Hi Ismael, Your example makes sense to me, where the individuals on the transect line are more or less beyond the scope of the detector (you in the plane).  It is physically impossible to see them.  B

messages.subject: Re: Back-transforming covariate coefficients with offsets
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ian,
I saw how you modeled extra survey effort as an offset in the linear model for lambda (supposedly because it exposed more of the population to sampling).  However, I was wondering what the advantage or differences would be in using a coefficent instead in the observation of counts
For example
log(lamda[s]) = ....linear model here, no effort offset
nobs[s] ~ dbinom(lambda[s]*effort) where effort is described in units, such as square kilometers surveyed.

In my case, I am dealing with line transects that vary in length and I interpret lambda as a "unit abundance", mean number per square kilometer.

On Saturday, May 30, 2020 at 9:19:45 AM UTC-6, Ian A. wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I fit a hierarchical community distance sampling model with latent abundances modeled as:
>
> log(lambda) <- points[s] + alpha[i] + beta[i,habitat[s]] + region[s]
>
> where:
> i = species,
> s = point count transect,
> points = offset for the log number of points surveyed in a given transect (sampling effort),
> alpha = species-specific intercept drawn from a community hyperdistribution,
> habitat = forests v. fragment (reference level is forest), and
> region is a random effect to account for environmental differences among sampling regions.
>
> I extracted the coefficients for beta, which represent the relative change in abundance between the fragment habitat class and forest. I'd like to back-transform those coefficients so that for each species I can say something like "Percent change in abundance compared to forest", etc. I'm unsure how to do so given the species intercept and offset for sampling effort.
>
> Many thanks in advance,
> Ian Ausprey

messages.subject: use of a random effect in a binomial mixed effects model
messages.subject_clean: use of a random effect in a binomial mixed effects model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all:

I am trying to fit a seemingly simple GLM through WinBUGS but
am having trouble wrapping my head around the appropriate model structure.

I have 90 data sets collected by independent researchers on
a variety of fish species (30 species total).
Each data set contains numbers of individuals experiencing mortality and
also numbers studied.  So, the response
data are binomially distributed.  There
are multiple data sets for some species but just one data set for other
species.  It makes sense for me to
consider species as a random effect in either a random intercepts or a random
coefficients model, as laid out in Kery’s Introduction to WinBUGS Chapter 12
(but using the logit link for the binomially distributed response data: chapter
19).  Considering species as a random
effect makes sense given the usual arguments for a random effect and given that
the same species is common to some of the 90 data sets.

I would like to determine whether each of two factors is a
meaningful covariate of the response data.
One factor is categorical (what type of collection gear the researcher
used, call it H), with two levels.  The
other factor is continuous (a life history trait, call it K).  However, for this continuous factor K, there is
only one value for species.  Put another
way, for each species, there is no contrast in a trait that may nonetheless
covary with the response.

For a random coefficients model, it doesn’t make sense for
me to have a likelihood such as

for (I in
1:n) {

C[i]
~dbin(p[i], N[i])

logit(p[i])
<- alpha[species[i]] + beta1[species[i]]*K[i] + beta2*H[i]

}

because, again, there is only 1 value of K per species.   Eliminating K from the model would be eliminating
a factor that might explain the response data.  In contrast,
retaining K in the model while getting rid of the species indicator also does
not seem to make sense due to lack of contrast in the K data for each species,
and due to the fact that there are multiple data sets for some species.

Thank you for any suggestions or ideas on appropriate model
structures to consider.

Paul Rudershausen

messages.subject_clean: use of a random effect in a binomial mixed effects model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Perhaps you should consider the example of site-occupancy modeling for multiple species.
If I understand you well, I think you need 1) a loop that passes through 1: S species to estimate the species-specific e.g. p, and then 2) create a vector with 1:S species to relate with the trait K.

Cheers,
André
